questions.stem:
The day of the ball arrived. Mme Loisel was a great success. She was the prettiest of all — elegant, gracious, smiling and full of joy. All the men noticed her, asked her name, and wanted to be presented. She danced with enthusiasm, intoxicated with pleasure, thinking of nothing but all this admiration, this victory so complete and sweet to her heart.

Which option best explains why Matilda felt that the evening had been a complete victory for her? (A) All the men at the ball had noticed her and wanted to be presented to her. (B) Her husband had told her that everybody wished for an invitation like it. (C) She had spent the whole evening thinking of the four hundred francs her husband had saved. (D) Mme Forestier had been present at the ball to admire the necklace she had lent.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: All the men at the ball had noticed her and wanted to be presented to her.

Mme Forestier stopped short. She said, “You say that you bought a diamond necklace to replace mine?” “Yes. You did not perceive it then? questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Your friend has a dress ready for a party but nothing to wear round her neck, and a rich friend has offered to lend her jewels for the evening. Write a letter of advice to your friend in about 100 words, saying what you would suggest she do.

markingPoints.description: Content: advises the friend to accept the loan of jewels and gives a clear reason for doing so.
Content: sets out practical precautions such as counting the jewels, noting the clasp, keeping the necklace on and checking it in the carriage.
Format: opens with a greeting and closes with a polite sign-off, as a letter must.
Organisation: the ideas run in order, from the advice to the two precautions, then a warning and a closing instruction.
Accuracy and expression: correct spelling and punctuation, with a clear direct style in about 100 words.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Dear Friend,
Do accept the loan, and make two promises before you go. First, count the stones and note every detail of the clasp, so you can describe the necklace exactly if it is ever lost. Second, keep it on your neck the whole evening and check it in the carriage before you reach home. I know a woman who borrowed a necklace, lost it, and spent ten years washing floors to pay for a debt. Enjoy your evening, but do not let one happy night turn into ten hard years. Tell your family the moment you are home.
Yours sincerely,
Your classmate

evidence: I am vexed not to have a jewel, nothing to adorn myself with.
Go and find your friend Mme Forestier and ask her to lend you her jewels.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: After a borrowed necklace of diamonds is lost on the way home from a party, the man who lost it decides to publish an advertisement in a Paris newspaper. Write that advertisement in about 100 words. Begin with a suitable heading and end with a clear line telling a finder what to do.

markingPoints.description: Content: states clearly what was lost and gives the place and the night on which it was lost.
Content: explains how the necklace can be recognised and what has already been done in the search for it.
Format: begins with a heading in capitals and reads as a newspaper advertisement.
Organisation: the notice moves from the loss, to the search already made, to what a finder must do.
Accuracy and expression: correct spelling and punctuation, with a formal public tone in about 100 words.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
LOST: A SUPERB NECKLACE OF DIAMONDS
Between the Minister's residence and our own door, on the night of the ball, a superb necklace of diamonds was lost. It had been lent to us by a dear friend, and its loss has ruined a family that cannot afford to replace it. We have already searched the whole track we walked on foot, and the police and the cab offices know nothing. The necklace may be recognised at once by anyone who saw it worn at the ball. Whoever finds it is asked to bring it to the police or to return it to M. Loisel, and a reward will be paid without fail for its return.

evidence: He went to the police and to the cab offices, and put an advertisement in the newspapers, offering a reward.
Suddenly she discovered, in a black satin box, a superb necklace of diamonds.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write a paragraph of about 100 words on what you have learnt from the life of a woman who borrowed jewels for one evening and then had to pay for them for ten years, and say what you would do if you ever lost something that did not belong to you.

markingPoints.description: Content: states the central moral, that one evening of pleasure can ruin many years of a family's life.
Content: gives the sequence of events, namely the borrowed necklace, the loss in the cab, the lie about a clasp and the ten years of payment.
Format: a single continuous paragraph of about 100 words, with no headings, numbering or letter layout.
Organisation: the ideas are linked in cause-and-effect order and end with the writer's own decision.
Accuracy and expression: correct spelling and punctuation, with simple connected sentences.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: One evening of pleasure can cost a lifetime of labour. The woman I have in mind borrowed a necklace, danced the whole night in it, and lost it in the cab on the way home. Because she told a lie about a broken clasp, she had to buy another that looked exactly the same, and the debt took ten years to clear. In those years she gave up her maid, moved into an attic and washed dishes, while her husband copied books at night. Honesty is cheaper than pride: if I lost something that was not mine, I would tell the owner at once.

evidence: It was necessary to pay this frightful debt. She would pay it.
And this life lasted for ten years. At the end of ten years, they had restored all.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Trace, step by step, how the loss of the borrowed necklace changed the life of the household, and say what their life was like before it was lost.

markingPoints.description: Before the loss they were poor but not in debt: he was a clerk at the Board of Education and she only suffered from the want of frocks and jewels.
She borrowed a diamond necklace from Mme Forestier and was the prettiest of all at the ball.
The necklace was lost in the cab; the dress, cloak and pockets were searched and the track on foot was walked over again.
M. Loisel went to the police and the cab offices and advertised a reward in the newspapers, but found nothing.
An identical necklace was bought for thirty-six thousand francs, the rest being borrowed from money-lenders.
They sent away the maid, took rooms in an attic, did the kitchen work themselves and lived like this for ten years, until the debt was cleared.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. Before the loss they were poor but not in debt: M. Loisel was a clerk at the Board of Education, and his wife suffered only from the want of frocks and jewels.
2. She borrowed a diamond necklace from Mme Forestier and was the prettiest of all at the ball.
3. In the cab home the necklace was lost; the dress, cloak and pockets were searched.
4. M. Loisel walked back over the track they had gone on foot, went to the police and the cab offices, and advertised a reward.
5. Nothing was found, so they bought an identical necklace for thirty-six thousand francs, borrowing the rest from money-lenders.
6. They sent away the maid, took rooms in an attic and did the kitchen work themselves for ten years, until the debt was cleared.

evidence: He went to the police and to the cab offices, and put an advertisement in the newspapers, offering a reward.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: In the last few lines a friend tells the heroine that the necklace she lent was false. Why does this come as a shock to the reader, and what does it suggest about the ten years the family spent paying for it?

markingPoints.description: The replacement necklace was valued at forty thousand francs and bought for thirty-six thousand.
The family paid by sending away the maid, moving to an attic, doing the kitchen work, and the husband copying at five sous a page.
The friend then admits that her own necklace was false and not worth over five hundred francs.
A fortune was therefore spent on an imitation of a worthless jewel, which is the source of the reader's shock.
It shows how one evening's desire to appear rich can be carried to ruin.
It throws doubt on the wife's claim that all her misery was caused by her friend, for the fault lay in her own pride.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. The reader has already been shown the price: the replacement necklace was valued at forty thousand francs and bought for thirty-six thousand.
2. To pay it the family gave up its maid, moved into an attic, did the kitchen work, and had the husband copy pages at five sous by night.
3. Then the friend admits that her own necklace was false and not worth over five hundred francs.
4. So the whole sacrifice rests on costume jewellery, and the sum paid was many times its real value.
5. The shock shows how far one evening's wish to appear rich can be carried.
6. It also casts doubt on the wife's claim that all her misery was caused by her friend, for the fault lay in her own pride.

evidence: It was valued at forty thousand francs. They could get it for thirty-six thousand.
Mine were false. They were not worth over five hundred francs!

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Both M. Loisel and Mme Loisel are changed by what happens. Show, step by step, how each of them changes, and say which of the two changes more.

markingPoints.description: She begins as a simple, unhappy young woman who dreams only of frocks and jewels.
At the ball she is the prettiest of all and thinks of nothing but admiration.
After the loss she sends away the maid, moves to an attic, washes dishes, carries refuse to the street and haggles to the last sou.
After ten years she has become a strong, hard woman, with red hands, a loud voice and her hair badly dressed.
He begins as a loving husband who gives her the four hundred francs saved for his gun, and later borrows from money-lenders and copies at five sous a page.
She changes more than he does, because her looks, her manner and her daily work are all altered by the debt.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. Mme Loisel begins as a simple, unhappy young woman who only dreams of frocks and jewels.
2. At the ball she is the prettiest of all, dancing while she thinks of nothing but admiration.
3. After the loss she sends away the maid, takes rooms in an attic, learns kitchen work, carries the refuse to the street and haggles to the last sou.
4. Ten years later she is a strong, hard woman, with red hands, a loud voice and her hair badly dressed.
5. M. Loisel begins as a loving husband who gives her the four hundred francs he had saved for his gun.
6. He borrows from money-lenders, works evenings putting books in order and copies at five sous a page; she changes more than he does.
